summary: The cmd_vel safety filter gains a scan watchdog: with no LaserScan for scan_timeout it publishes a zero Twist instead of forwarding commands on stale data, and the hard-coded stop distance becomes the stop_distance parameter.

questions.question: What does the node publish on /cmd_vel once no /scan message has arrived for longer than scan_timeout?
questions.rubric: A zero Twist (full stop) from the watchdog branch in _on_cmd_vel, with a throttled warning; it never forwards the incoming command or repeats the last one.

rules.feedback: Correct: the watchdog publishes an empty Twist, a full stop, not the incoming command.
Correct: the watchdog publishes an empty Twist, a full stop, not the incoming command.
Right outcome; say what it publishes: a zero Twist, not the last command.
The opposite: it publishes Twist(), never the last command.

default.feedback: No answer that describes the watchdog output.

questions.question: Why is the staleness check done in the cmd_vel callback rather than in the scan callback?
questions.rubric: The scan callback never runs once scans stop arriving, so a check there could not fire; the cmd_vel path keeps executing as long as someone is driving, so that is where the watchdog must live.

rules.feedback: Yes: once scans stop, _on_scan never runs, so the check has to live on the path that still executes.
Yes: the cmd_vel callback keeps running while _on_scan goes silent.
A timer would work too; the point is that _on_scan cannot detect its own absence.

default.feedback: Missed: a callback that has stopped firing cannot notice that it stopped.

questions.question: The lidar is healthy but its clock runs a few seconds behind the robot's. What does the robot do?
questions.rubric: Age is computed from header.stamp against the node clock, so every scan looks older than scan_timeout: the watchdog fires on each command and the robot refuses to move.

rules.feedback: Exactly: every scan looks stale because age is header.stamp against the node clock, so it never moves.
Exactly: the watchdog fires on every command and the robot refuses to move.
Right, and the consequence: every scan looks older than scan_timeout, so the watchdog fires on every single command.
It matters: the age check uses header.stamp, not arrival time.

default.feedback: Missed: age comes from header.stamp, so clock skew changes behaviour.

questions.question: Which new parameter controls the obstacle stop, and what happens if it is set to 0?
questions.rubric: stop_distance replaces the STOP_DISTANCE constant; at 0 the min_range < stop_distance test can never be true, so the obstacle stop is silently disabled.

rules.feedback: Correct: stop_distance, and at 0 the comparison can never be true, so the obstacle stop is off.
Name it: stop_distance. At 0 the obstacle stop is silently disabled.

default.feedback: Missed: stop_distance is new and 0 turns the obstacle stop off.

questions.question: How would you test the watchdog without a real lidar?
questions.rubric: Publish synthetic LaserScan messages from a test node, stop publishing, send a cmd_vel_raw and assert /cmd_vel is a zero Twist; launch_testing or an rclpy test with a fake or sim clock keeps it repeatable.

rules.feedback: Good: launch_testing with a synthetic scan publisher makes the watchdog a repeatable check.
Good: publish fake scans, stop, send a command, assert a zero Twist on /cmd_vel.
Good: publish fake scans, stop, send a command, assert a zero Twist on /cmd_vel.
Simulation works; a small test node publishing scans is faster and runs in CI.
Driving it by hand is not a repeatable check; publish synthetic scans in a test.
